props.title: Burlesque
props.initialSlug: Small-town girl chases burlesque stardom in LA

sections.content: Burlesque marks a fascinating intersection of modern musical spectacle and classic showbiz drama, following the tradition of backstage musicals like Cabaret (1972) and Chicago (2002). Christina Aguilera's Ali channels the wide-eyed ambition of Renée Zellweger's Roxie Hart, while Cher's Tess embodies the world-weary wisdom of previous grande dames like Bette Davis in All About Eve (1950). The film's glitzy aesthetic and elaborate musical numbers pay homage to the golden age of Hollywood musicals while updating the format for contemporary audiences.

sections.content: The film's neo-burlesque setting taps into a cultural revival that gained momentum in the 2000s, alongside documentaries like A Wink and a Smile (2008) and performances by Dita Von Teese. Director Steve Antin crafts elaborate musical sequences that blend contemporary pop with classic burlesque aesthetics, though critics noted the sanitized PG-13 approach compared to grittier predecessors like Cabaret (1972) or even Flashdance (1983).

Cher's return to the screen after a seven-year absence echoes other comeback vehicles like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and The Last of Sheila (1973), where aging performers confront changing entertainment landscapes. Her character Tess's struggle to keep her club alive mirrors real-world tensions between traditional performance venues and modern development, themes also explored in Coyote Ugly (2000) and Rock of Ages (2012). sections.content: Burlesque arrived during a renaissance of movie musicals, following the success of Chicago (2002) and preceding films like Les Misérables (2012) and La La Land (2016). Its emphasis on female empowerment through performance art connects it to films like Hustlers (2019) and Birds of Prey (2020), though with less edge and more sequins. The film's soundtrack, featuring Christina Aguilera's powerful vocals, continues the tradition of pop stars crossing over to film, like Diana Ross in Lady Sings the Blues (1972) and Madonna in Evita (1996).
